input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.

Topic: CSCI-536: Information Retrieval. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: An introduction to the theories and techniques used to construct search engines. Topics include search interfaces, traditional retrieval models (e.g., TF-IDF, BM25), modern retrieval techniques (e.g., neural reranking and retrieval), search engine evaluation, and search applications (e.g., conversational IR, enterprise search). Students will also review current IR research topics, and complete a group project in which they will design and execute experiments for search engine components. Prerequisites: CSCI-331 or equivalent course. Students may not take and receive credit for CSCI-536 and CSCI-636. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Spring

Source excerpts:

[nist-ai-rmf]
The NIST AI Risk Management Framework organizes work around Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. Govern establishes policies, responsibilities, and accountability for AI risk. Map documents context, intended use, affected people, and potential impacts. Measure uses qualitative and quantitative methods to analyze identified risks. Manage prioritizes risks and allocates resources for response and monitoring. Risk analysis considers data quality and uncertainty. It also considers robustness, privacy, security, transparency, and fairness. Monitoring continues after deployment because context and system behavior can change.

[rit-csci-536]
An introduction to the theories and techniques used to construct search engines. Topics include search interfaces, traditional retrieval models (e.g., TF-IDF, BM25), modern retrieval techniques (e.g., neural reranking and retrieval), search engine evaluation, and search applications (e.g., conversational IR, enterprise search). Students will also review current IR research topics, and complete a group project in which they will design and execute experiments for search engine components. Prerequisites: CSCI-331 or equivalent course. Students may not take and receive credit for CSCI-536 and CSCI-636. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Spring

[scikit-learn-user-guide]
Machine-learning workflows separate data preparation, training, validation, testing, model selection, and evaluation. Supervised methods learn a mapping from examples paired with target labels. Unsupervised methods identify structure without target labels. Preprocessing must be fitted only on permitted training data to avoid leakage. Pipelines combine preprocessing and estimators so the same transformations are applied consistently. Cross-validation repeats training and validation across defined data splits. Evaluation metrics must match the task and the cost of different errors. Hyperparameter selection must remain separate from final test evaluation. Leakage, distribution shift, overfitting, and unexamined assumptions can invalidate results.

beats.claim: A search engine pipeline consists of indexing, retrieval, and ranking stages that transform raw documents into ranked results for user queries.
beats.example: When a user searches for 'climate change policies', the system first retrieves relevant documents from an index, then ranks them based on relevance before displaying the top results.
beats.title: Search Engine Pipeline Overview
beats.visualDirection: Display a horizontal flowchart with three labeled boxes: 'Query Input', 'Index & Retrieval', and 'Ranking & Output', connected by arrows indicating data flow.

beats.claim: Traditional retrieval models like TF-IDF and BM25 calculate document relevance using statistical measures of term frequency and inverse document frequency.
beats.example: TF-IDF assigns higher scores to terms that appear frequently in a specific document but rarely across the entire corpus, while BM25 adjusts for document length and term saturation.
beats.title: Traditional Retrieval Models
beats.visualDirection: Show a side-by-side comparison table listing 'TF-IDF' and 'BM25', with columns for 'Core Mechanism', 'Key Formula Components', and 'Typical Use Case'.

beats.claim: Modern retrieval techniques employ neural reranking and retrieval models that use deep learning to capture semantic meaning and contextual relationships in text.
beats.example: A neural reranker re-scores initially retrieved documents by analyzing query-document interactions through transformer-based architectures, improving relevance for complex or ambiguous queries.
beats.title: Modern Neural Retrieval
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a two-stage pipeline: a traditional retriever outputs a candidate set, which is then passed to a neural reranker that outputs a refined ranked list.

beats.claim: Search interfaces design how users interact with retrieval systems, balancing simplicity with advanced features like autocomplete, filters, and conversational prompts.
beats.example: A conversational IR interface allows users to ask natural language questions, while an enterprise search interface provides faceted navigation and role-based access controls.
beats.title: Search Interfaces
beats.visualDirection: Display mockups of two search interfaces: one with a simple text box and autocomplete dropdown, and another with a chat-style prompt and structured filters.

beats.claim: Search engine evaluation uses standardized metrics to measure retrieval quality, ensuring that improvements align with user needs and system constraints.
beats.example: Precision, recall, and mean average precision (MAP) quantify how many relevant documents appear in the top results, while user satisfaction surveys assess perceived usefulness.
beats.title: Search Engine Evaluation
beats.visualDirection: Present a bar chart comparing precision and recall scores across three different retrieval models, with a legend indicating model names.

beats.claim: Search applications extend beyond basic retrieval to include conversational IR, enterprise search, and domain-specific systems that integrate with broader software ecosystems.
beats.example: Conversational IR systems maintain dialogue state and context to answer follow-up questions, while enterprise search integrates with CRM and document management platforms.
beats.title: Search Applications
beats.visualDirection: Create a Venn diagram showing overlapping circles for 'Conversational IR', 'Enterprise Search', and 'Domain-Specific Search', with intersection labels indicating shared features like context awareness and integration capabilities.

beats.claim: Machine learning workflows for information retrieval separate data preparation, training, validation, and testing to prevent data leakage and ensure model generalization.
beats.example: Preprocessing steps like tokenization and vectorization are fitted only on training data, while cross-validation ensures consistent evaluation across multiple data splits.
beats.title: Machine Learning Workflows in IR
beats.visualDirection: Show a sequential diagram of a machine learning pipeline with labeled stages: 'Data Preparation', 'Training', 'Validation', 'Testing', and 'Model Selection', with arrows indicating forward flow.

beats.claim: Evaluation metrics must match the task and the cost of different errors, and common failure modes like leakage, distribution shift, and overfitting can invalidate results.
beats.example: Using accuracy for ranking tasks often masks poor performance on long-tail queries, while distribution shift between training and test data reduces model reliability in production.
beats.title: Evaluation Metrics and Error Analysis
beats.visualDirection: Display a checklist graphic with items like 'Metric-Task Alignment', 'Leakage Prevention', 'Distribution Shift Detection', and 'Overfitting Monitoring', each with a checkbox.

beats.claim: Current IR research focuses on improving retrieval accuracy, reducing latency, and developing robust systems that handle uncertainty and fairness constraints.
beats.example: Researchers design experiments to compare neural reranking strategies under varying query complexity, measuring improvements in MAP and latency while monitoring for bias in ranked results.
beats.title: Research Topics and Experiment Design
beats.visualDirection: Present a template for an experiment design card with fields for 'Hypothesis', 'Variables', 'Metrics', 'Constraints', and 'Expected Outcomes', formatted as a structured form.

beats.claim: A practical analysis checklist ensures that search engine components are evaluated for correctness, efficiency, and alignment with user and system requirements before deployment.
beats.example: Instructors and developers use the checklist to verify that indexing covers all required fields, retrieval models are tuned for the target domain, and evaluation metrics reflect real-world performance.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Show a printable checklist graphic with sections for 'Indexing Verification', 'Retrieval Tuning', 'Evaluation Validation', and 'Deployment Readiness', each containing three actionable items.

learningObjectives: Define and explain the core components of a search engine pipeline, including indexing, retrieval, and ranking.
Compare traditional statistical retrieval models (TF-IDF, BM25) with modern neural retrieval techniques and their respective strengths.
Apply standard evaluation metrics to assess search engine performance and identify common failure modes like data leakage or distribution shift.
